title: The impact of air temperature, relative humidity, and solar irradiance on ultramarathon running speed in women and men
authors: Struska M, Hora M, Wall-Scheffler C, Sladek V
population: 1,353,878 finish times in 8,582 ultramarathons of 50-161 km at daily-average air temperature 0-34 C, relative humidity 0-100% and solar irradiance 0-700 W/m2
findings: Running speed declined in both sexes at high air temperature, with a steeper decline in men, narrowing the speed difference between sexes from 0.73 km/h at 0-8 C to 0.34 km/h at 34 C.
The narrowing was most pronounced at high humidity: predicted difference 0.21 km/h at 34 C and 90% RH.
Relative humidity had the opposite but weaker effect on the sex difference (+0.07 km/h across its range).
Solar irradiance had a small effect on running speed with no significant sex difference.
limitations: Abstract only (online ahead of print, 2026); daily-averaged air temperature, not WBGT or hour-by-hour; aggregate race-level data; no per-degree slope for the whole field stated in the abstract; no zero-citation record yet.
implications: First large ultra-specific dataset: heat slows both sexes in 50-161 km races, so ultras need a heat term, but the abstract gives no per-degree slope for plan use.

Men lose more speed than women at high air temperature in ultras; treat a sex term as a low-confidence calibration covariate, not a hard-coded penalty. It also qualifies Vihma 2010's marathon statement.
Solar irradiance mattered little for ultra speed here, so do not over-weight solar load for ultras (WBGT still captures it).

verification.notes: Added by verifier: very recent (2026) large ultra dataset. Crossref (MSSE online 2026-09-17, Struska first author) and Europe PMC abstract (PMID 42750656) re-fetched. Preprint-era; replicate before heavy reliance.
